science.geologic-units-stratigraphy.explain: Like pages in a book, rock layers stack over time, with ejecta (material thrown out of craters) blanketing older surfaces. The USGS Unified Geologic Map of the Moon, which outlines these units, is not yet loaded.
science.geologic-units-stratigraphy.readIt: Once available, more distinct units nearby means richer samples for reconstructing lunar history.

science.rock-composition-spectral-minera.lead: This would tell us which minerals and rock types make up the surface around the site.
science.rock-composition-spectral-minera.explain: Orbiting instruments identify minerals by the pattern of light they reflect, since each has its own spectral fingerprint. Near the pole the Sun is low and shadows are long, so these orbital maps are unreliable there and have not been loaded.
science.rock-composition-spectral-minera.readIt: Once available, a wider variety of materials would mean more science diversity and potential resources.

science.geologic-age-crater-chronology.lead: This would tell us roughly how old the surface at this site is.
science.geologic-age-crater-chronology.explain: Older surfaces have faced impacts longer, so they collect more craters, like pavement gathering more raindrop spots the longer it rains. Estimating an age needs crater counts for the local surface unit, which the app lacks.
science.geologic-age-crater-chronology.readIt: Once available, an older age points to material recording early lunar history, and the uncertainty matters as much as the number.

science.permanently-shadowed-region-psr-.lead: Around this site, the permanent-shadow check finds {value}.
science.permanently-shadowed-region-psr-.explain: With the Sun always low at the pole, deep crater floors and ground behind ridges can stay dark for very long periods, becoming extremely cold traps where ice may collect. The app simulates one year, but true PSRs are defined over an 18.6-year cycle, so this slightly over-counts.
science.permanently-shadowed-region-psr-.readIt: More shadowed area means more potential ice targets, but those spots are dark and frigid to work in.

science.psr-access-distance-and-difficul.lead: With your mission settings, reaching the nearest cold trap means {value}.
science.psr-access-distance-and-difficul.explain: A rover heading into a cold trap must cover the distance, handle slopes, then work in darkness with no sunlight for its solar panels. The app converts distance into drive time and energy using your rover settings; Wh (watt-hours) measures energy, like battery capacity.
science.psr-access-distance-and-difficul.readIt: Shorter drives and less energy mean easier cold-trap science; larger values eat into power, time and margins.

science.hydrogen-proxy-concentration.lead: This would tell us whether orbital instruments see hints of hydrogen, a possible sign of water-rich material, near the site.
science.hydrogen-proxy-concentration.explain: Cosmic rays knock neutrons out of the surface, and hydrogen soaks up their energy, so fewer escaping neutrons hints at more hydrogen, possibly in ice. It is a clue, not an ice measurement; the LEND and Lunar Prospector neutron maps are not yet loaded.
science.hydrogen-proxy-concentration.readIt: Once available, stronger neutron suppression means more hydrogen, but not how much ice or in what form.

science.water-ice-abundance-estimate.lead: This would tell us how much water ice might be mixed into the soil here, and at what depths.
science.water-ice-abundance-estimate.explain: Ice survives only in extremely cold places like permanently shadowed craters, and orbital estimates of its amount rely on indirect signals and models. There is no direct measurement at this site, and orbital estimates are too coarse to trust here.
science.water-ice-abundance-estimate.readIt: Once available, a higher ice fraction means a stronger resource prospect, though the uncertainty matters as much as the estimate.

science.ice-physical-state-and-depth.lead: This would tell us whether any ice is surface frost, grains mixed into the soil, or buried layers.
science.ice-physical-state-and-depth.explain: The form of ice matters as much as the amount: surface frost could be scraped up, while buried lenses (pockets of ice) need digging or drilling. Finding out requires instruments on the ground or radar sounding (radio waves bounced into the subsurface).
science.ice-physical-state-and-depth.readIt: Once available, shallow or exposed ice is easier to sample; deep ice needs heavier hardware.

science.cold-trap-thermal-stability.lead: For this site, the cold-trap check reports {value}.
science.cold-trap-thermal-stability.explain: Ice that gets too warm slowly turns straight into vapour and drifts away, so it lasts only where even the maximum temperature stays very low. The site itself is usually sunlit, so the best cold traps lie in nearby shadowed regions.
science.cold-trap-thermal-stability.readIt: A colder maximum means ice survives longer, and a closer PSR means those cold traps are easier to reach.

science.other-volatiles-organics.lead: This would tell us which frozen substances besides water, such as carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide or ammonia, might be trapped here.
science.other-volatiles-organics.explain: Volatiles (substances that turn into gas easily) can freeze out in the coldest shadowed spots, where they carry science value and hints of interesting chemistry. Identifying them needs measurements made on the surface.
science.other-volatiles-organics.readIt: Once available, a richer mix of species would raise the site's science value.

science.resource-extraction-feasibility.lead: This would tell us whether local ice or other materials could be dug up and turned into useful supplies, and at what energy cost.
science.resource-extraction-feasibility.explain: Finding ice is only step one: ISRU (in-situ resource utilisation, making supplies from local materials) also depends on digging depth, energy needed and yield. Estimating that needs ice abundance and extraction hardware assumptions.
science.resource-extraction-feasibility.readIt: Once available, higher yield for less energy means a more practical resource site.

science.science-diversity-score.lead: Around this site, the science variety count is {value}.
science.science-diversity-score.explain: A site near many kinds of features, such as craters, mountains and shadowed regions, lets one mission tackle several independent science questions. The app counts how many distinct feature types lie nearby.
science.science-diversity-score.readIt: A higher count means more objectives from one landing, though a low count can still suit a single-goal mission.

science.instrument-deployment-suitabilit.lead: With your mission settings, the deployment check gives: {value}.
science.instrument-deployment-suitabilit.explain: Instruments need a stable, fairly level base, the right lighting for power and sometimes a clear line of sight to Earth or the sky. The app checks local slope and sunlight against your mission settings.
science.instrument-deployment-suitabilit.readIt: Suitable means the basic conditions are met; unsuitable flags a problem, like steep ground or darkness, to solve first.

logistics.activity-timeline-critical-pat.lead: With your mission settings, the schedule check for this site and date gives: {value}.
logistics.activity-timeline-critical-pat.explain: A mission is a chain of tasks: setting up equipment, doing science, moving supplies and sending data home. Some steps need sunlight and an Earth link at once, so the planner lines up those windows like a timetable.
logistics.activity-timeline-critical-pat.readIt: A longer shared window leaves room to finish every task; none means splitting tasks up or reconsidering the date.

logistics.operational-mode-autonomy-rule.lead: Communication outlook for this site and date: {value}.
logistics.operational-mode-autonomy-rule.explain: When Earth drops below the local horizon, controllers cannot send commands, so the lander must follow stored instructions and switch to a protective safe mode if something goes wrong. Think of a house-sitter who must cope alone until the owners can be reached again.
logistics.operational-mode-autonomy-rule.readIt: Shorter required autonomy keeps the mission simple; long blackouts demand smarter onboard software and sturdier safe modes.

logistics.consumables-spares-reserves.lead: This would show how much propellant, power reactants, spare parts and life-support supplies a mission can use while keeping a safety reserve.
logistics.consumables-spares-reserves.explain: A mission carries a fixed stock of supplies, and its reserve decides how long it lasts and how well it copes with surprises. It depends on the mission's own design, not on site data.
logistics.consumables-spares-reserves.readIt: Bigger reserves would mean a longer, more resilient mission, but every extra kilogram must be launched and landed.

logistics.command-telemetry-buffer.lead: With your mission settings, the onboard data storage needed at this site is {value}.
logistics.command-telemetry-buffer.explain: While Earth is out of view, instruments keep collecting data that must be saved onboard until the link returns, like recording a show while you are away. The estimate multiplies the assumed data rate by the length of the longest blackout.
logistics.command-telemetry-buffer.readIt: A larger figure means carrying more memory or discarding data; a smaller one means science easily survives blackouts.

logistics.deployment-and-workspace-area.lead: Flat working room around this site: {value}.
logistics.deployment-and-workspace-area.explain: Antennas, solar arrays, instruments and rovers all need level ground with clearance around them, much like pitching a tent on flat ground. The area is measured from LRO LOLA laser-altimeter elevation maps by counting ground that is gentle enough.
logistics.deployment-and-workspace-area.readIt: More gentle area gives more freedom to lay out equipment; a small area forces a cramped or compromised layout.

logistics.anchor-structure-erectability.lead: This would tell us whether the ground can firmly hold masts, solar arrays and sensors once they are dug in or anchored.
logistics.anchor-structure-erectability.explain: Raising equipment higher can catch more sunlight or a better view of Earth, but a tall structure needs soil strong enough to carry its weight and resist tipping. That requires soil-strength measurements at the site, which are not yet available.
logistics.anchor-structure-erectability.readIt: Firmer ground would allow taller structures, while weak soil would limit how high equipment can safely stand.

logistics.ground-station-schedules-downl.explain: The DSN (NASA's Deep Space Network of giant radio dishes) must have the Moon above its horizon to talk to a lander. This counts only that geometry; real dish time is scheduled and shared with other missions, so seeing the Moon does not mean a dish is booked.
logistics.ground-station-schedules-downl.readIt: A higher share means more chances to book contact, but treat it as an upper limit, not a guarantee.

logistics.nearby-landings-plume-exclusio.explain: A landing rocket blasts dust and small rocks sideways at high speed, and with no air to slow them they can travel a long way. Keeping a buffer around other landings protects working equipment and historic sites from this spray.
logistics.nearby-landings-plume-exclusio.readIt: No nearby landings means little plume risk; a close neighbour would call for coordinated timing or a wider separation.

logistics.operational-safety-margins-res.lead: Time buffer at this site and date: {value}.
logistics.operational-safety-margins-res.explain: Near the south pole the Sun skims the horizon, so hills and crater rims can bring darkness, cold and power loss. The margin is the slack before the first such limit, like leaving early for a train in case of delays, worked out from NASA JPL Horizons Sun positions and LRO terrain.
logistics.operational-safety-margins-res.readIt: More slack lets the mission absorb delays; a thin margin leaves little room for anything to go wrong.

logistics.site-infrastructure-reuse-pote.lead: Infrastructure reuse outlook for this site: {value}.
logistics.site-infrastructure-reuse-pote.explain: Later missions save effort if they can share earlier relays, power pads or cleared paths, much as a new town grows faster beside an existing road. This looks for previous landings close enough to build on.
logistics.site-infrastructure-reuse-pote.readIt: Nearby earlier hardware raises reuse potential for a long campaign, while a fresh site offers a clean start but nothing to share.

rover.traversable-slope-cross-slope.explain: A rover can slip or tip over on steep ground, especially when driving sideways across a slope. The limit used here is the slope capability of NASA's VIPER rover, and slopes come from LRO LOLA elevation maps.
rover.traversable-slope-cross-slope.readIt: A higher share of gentle ground means freedom to drive almost anywhere; a low share means routes must detour around steep patches.

rover.route-obstacle-density.lead: This would count how often rocks and craters too large to cross block a rover's path.
rover.route-obstacle-density.explain: Even gentle terrain can be scattered with boulders and small craters that force detours, like furniture in a dark room. Measuring this needs boulder and crater maps detailed to the metre scale, which are not yet included.
rover.route-obstacle-density.readIt: Fewer obstacles per kilometre would mean straighter, faster routes; more would mean longer detours and more planning.

rover.route-length-and-cumulative-ascent.lead: Distance from this site to the nearest permanently shadowed region: {value}.
rover.route-length-and-cumulative-ascent.explain: A PSR (permanently shadowed region, a crater floor sunlight never reaches) is the rover target used here. This is a straight-line distance, so a real route winding around hills and climbing slopes will be longer, costing more time, energy and wheel wear.
rover.route-length-and-cumulative-ascent.readIt: Shorter is easier, but treat the figure as a minimum rather than the actual drive.

rover.travel-speed-slip.lead: With your mission settings, the rover speed and one-way drive time are {value}.
rover.travel-speed-slip.explain: Rovers pause often to check for hazards and plan the next stretch, and loose soil or slopes make wheels slip. Dividing the distance by the assumed speed turns a map distance into a schedule.
rover.travel-speed-slip.readIt: A faster speed shortens the trip and saves energy, but if slip or navigation pauses are worse than assumed, the drive takes longer.

rover.traverse-energy-consumption.lead: With your mission settings, the estimated energy for the drive there and back is {value}.
rover.traverse-energy-consumption.explain: Driving uses electricity for motors, heaters and computers, and the cost grows with distance and climbing. Like a phone on a long day out, the rover must keep enough charge to get home, so the round trip plus margin sets how far science can reach.
rover.traverse-energy-consumption.readIt: Lower energy fits comfortably in the rover's budget; higher energy limits range or demands recharging stops.

rover.dynamic-sunlight-along-route.lead: Sunlight around this site during the mission: {value}.
rover.dynamic-sunlight-along-route.explain: At the south pole the Sun circles low near the horizon, so shadows from hills and crater rims sweep across the ground and a spot lit now may be dark later. Sun positions from NASA JPL Horizons are combined with LRO terrain to track lighting over time.
rover.dynamic-sunlight-along-route.readIt: A higher percentage means a solar-powered rover is less likely to drive into long shadow; a lower one means drives must be timed carefully.

rover.dynamic-communications-along-route.explain: To be commanded directly, a moving rover needs Earth above its local horizon, and at the south pole Earth hangs low, so nearby hills can block it. DTE (direct-to-Earth radio contact) is checked across the area using JPL Horizons Earth positions and LRO terrain.
rover.dynamic-communications-along-route.readIt: A higher percentage means more chances to command and hear from the rover; a low one means long drives without direct contact unless a relay is used.

rover.safe-haven-waypoints.lead: Nearest safe spot to rest and recharge: {value}.
rover.safe-haven-waypoints.explain: A rover caught in darkness can run out of power and get dangerously cold, so planners look for nearby spots that are both gently sloped and well lit, like a refuge hut for mountain climbers. The search uses LRO terrain and computed lighting.
rover.safe-haven-waypoints.readIt: A closer, sunnier haven is a safer fallback; a distant or dim one leaves the rover more exposed during dark or blackout periods.

rover.route-temporal-feasibility-return-.lead: With your mission settings, the round-trip timing check gives: {value}.
rover.route-temporal-feasibility-return-.explain: This combines drive time, energy and lighting into one go/no-go question: can the rover reach its target and get back before darkness or other limits close in? It is like checking that a hike there and back fits before nightfall.
rover.route-temporal-feasibility-return-.readIt: A comfortable return margin means the traverse works; no margin means shortening the route, driving faster or picking another date.

rover.localization-navigation-uncertaint.lead: This would show how precisely a rover knows where it is while driving through areas with few recognisable landmarks.
rover.localization-navigation-uncertaint.explain: A rover estimates its position by tracking what its cameras see and how far its wheels turn, and small errors add up where landmarks are scarce or hidden in shadow. It is not shown because it depends on the rover's own sensors and software.
rover.localization-navigation-uncertaint.readIt: Smaller uncertainty would mean safer, more confident driving; larger uncertainty means wider safety buffers around hazards.

rover.visibility-visual-ergonomics.lead: Lighting for cameras and drivers at this site and date: {value}.
rover.visibility-visual-ergonomics.explain: With the Sun barely above the horizon, even a small rock casts a very long shadow, and with no air to scatter light, shadows are pitch black beside dazzling sunlit ground. That harsh contrast and glare make hazards hard for cameras and operators to spot.
rover.visibility-visual-ergonomics.readIt: A higher Sun means shorter shadows and easier viewing; a lower Sun means longer shadows that can hide or exaggerate hazards.

rover.route-science-yield-vs-cost.lead: This would rate how much science a route delivers for the distance, time and power it costs.
rover.route-science-yield-vs-cost.explain: Planners weigh each target's scientific value against the effort to reach it, like choosing which museum rooms to visit with only an afternoon. It needs agreed science objectives and their relative importance, which this tool does not have yet.
rover.route-science-yield-vs-cost.readIt: A higher score would mean more science per unit of effort, helping choose between a nearby modest target and a distant valuable one.

space-weather.solar-energetic-particle-s.lead: Across the Moon, the radiation dose from a large solar particle event is typically {value}.
space-weather.solar-energetic-particle-s.explain: A solar eruption can hurl energetic protons (charged particles) at the Moon, and with no atmosphere or global magnetic field they reach the surface directly. These values assume average shielding; most events are far weaker.
space-weather.solar-energetic-particle-s.readIt: It is the same for every site, so it does not rank locations; it tells planners how much shelter a strong solar storm demands.

space-weather.galactic-cosmic-ray-exposu.lead: Across the Moon, the highest cosmic-ray dose rate measured from lunar orbit is {value}.
space-weather.galactic-cosmic-ray-exposu.explain: Galactic cosmic rays (fast particles from outside the solar system) arrive steadily from every direction, unblocked by air or magnetic field. LRO's CRaTER instrument measured this in orbit during a quiet-Sun period; on the surface the Moon blocks half the sky, roughly halving the dose.
space-weather.galactic-cosmic-ray-exposu.readIt: It does not rank sites; it is a baseline that adds up over time and shapes shielding for crews and electronics.

space-weather.radiation-dose-behind-shie.lead: This would estimate how much radiation actually reaches electronics or crew after passing through the spacecraft's shielding.
space-weather.radiation-dose-behind-shie.explain: Shielding material absorbs part of the incoming radiation, a bit like sunscreen blocking some sunlight. The result depends on the shield's material and thickness, which come from the mission design rather than from site data.
space-weather.radiation-dose-behind-shie.readIt: A lower dose behind shielding would mean longer hardware life and safer crews, at the cost of heavier shielding.

space-weather.surface-plasma-solar-wind-.lead: Across the Moon, the solar wind delivers a proton flux of typically {value}.
space-weather.surface-plasma-solar-wind-.explain: The solar wind is a constant stream of charged particles from the Sun that strikes the unprotected lunar surface directly. Sunlit ground stays close to neutral, but shadowed ground can charge to strongly negative voltages, so equipment moving between light and shadow can build up static charge.
space-weather.surface-plasma-solar-wind-.readIt: This Moon-wide value does not rank sites; it guides grounding and material choices, especially near sunlight-shadow boundaries.

space-weather.micrometeoroid-background-.lead: Across the Moon, the measured impact rate for meteoroids in the size range studied is {value}.
space-weather.micrometeoroid-background-.explain: With no atmosphere to burn them up, meteoroids hit the Moon at very high speed, and NASA estimates how often by counting the brief flashes of light they make on impact.
space-weather.micrometeoroid-background-.readIt: A tiny rate per square metre per year means a strike on any one lander is very unlikely; it is the same everywhere, so it shapes protective design rather than site choice.

space-weather.predictable-meteor-stream-.lead: This would show whether the Moon passes through a known meteor stream during the mission, briefly raising the impact rate.
space-weather.predictable-meteor-stream-.explain: Just as Earth gets meteor showers when it crosses a comet's dust trail, the Moon crosses the same streams and briefly receives extra impacts. These forecasts are not yet loaded into this tool.
space-weather.predictable-meteor-stream-.readIt: A higher ratio would mean more impacts during that interval, mainly useful for timing sensitive activities rather than choosing a site.

space-weather.known-asteroid-or-comet-lu.lead: This would show whether any catalogued asteroid or comet is predicted to strike the Moon near the site.
space-weather.known-asteroid-or-comet-lu.explain: Astronomers track asteroids and comets and can calculate whether a path might meet the Moon, though every prediction carries uncertainty. This is a rare-event watch, and no lunar-impact assessment feed is connected yet.
space-weather.known-asteroid-or-comet-lu.readIt: A meaningful probability near the site would be a reason for caution, but it is not a routine factor in choosing a site.

space-weather.recent-local-impact-detect.lead: Across the Moon, before-and-after orbital imaging has revealed {value} formed during the period studied.
space-weather.recent-local-impact-detect.explain: LROC (the cameras on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter) photographed the same places years apart, and comparing image pairs exposes fresh craters and ejecta (material thrown out by an impact), showing the surface is still changing.
space-weather.recent-local-impact-detect.readIt: This is a Moon-wide count, not a site result; a higher rate means maps age faster and fresh imagery matters more before landing.

space-weather.eclipse-occultation-by-orb.lead: Eclipse check for this site and mission window: {value}.
space-weather.eclipse-occultation-by-orb.explain: When Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, its shadow cuts off sunlight to solar panels and lets equipment cool quickly. Using Sun and Earth positions from NASA JPL Horizons, the tool looks for such interruptions during the mission.
space-weather.eclipse-occultation-by-orb.readIt: No eclipses means no power cuts from this cause; an eclipse adds a dark, cold spell the mission must be built to survive.

space-weather.radiation-impact-event-ale.lead: This would show how far to trust a space-weather or impact warning, including how much advance notice it gives.
space-weather.radiation-impact-event-ale.explain: Solar storms and impacts are hard to predict, so a warning comes with a probability and a lead time, much like a weather forecast. Without a live space-weather forecast feed, the tool avoids pretending to know more than it does.
space-weather.radiation-impact-event-ale.readIt: Higher confidence and longer lead time would let controllers act early; low confidence means planning for surprises.

heritage.previous-landing-impact-locatio.lead: Earlier spacecraft landings or impacts near this site: {value}.
heritage.previous-landing-impact-locatio.explain: Knowing where spacecraft have landed, crashed or attempted to touch down provides context, safety lessons and history. The tool checks this site against a curated list of past landing and impact coordinates.
heritage.previous-landing-impact-locatio.readIt: Nearby past visits add heritage and lessons but may call for keeping a respectful distance; none means unvisited ground.

heritage.mission-outcome-and-anomaly-his.lead: Recorded outcomes of earlier missions near this site: {value}.
heritage.mission-outcome-and-anomaly-his.explain: Past landings teach practical lessons: whether a lander tipped, lost power or lost contact, and why. These records help engineers avoid repeating mistakes and give students real stories to connect with the site.
heritage.mission-outcome-and-anomaly-his.readIt: Successes nearby build confidence and anomalies flag hazards worth studying; no entry means there is no local track record to learn from.

heritage.prior-orbital-coverage-repeat-i.explain: Before landing, planners rely on maps made from orbit, such as LOLA (a laser that measures surface height), LROC (cameras) and Diviner (which measures surface temperature). Repeated passes over the years build confidence and reveal changes.
heritage.prior-orbital-coverage-repeat-i.readIt: More frequent and sharper coverage means more trustworthy maps; thin coverage means more uncertainty about what is really on the ground.

heritage.prior-in-situ-chemistry-soil-ob.lead: Direct ground measurements of soil or chemistry near this site: {value}.
heritage.prior-in-situ-chemistry-soil-ob.explain: Orbital instruments infer what the surface is made of from a distance, so samples or sensor readings taken on the ground act as ground truth that checks those clues, like tasting a dish instead of judging it from a photo.
heritage.prior-in-situ-chemistry-soil-ob.readIt: Nearby measurements raise confidence in the maps; none means predictions for this site rest entirely on remote data.

heritage.documented-hazard-or-rover-trav.lead: Documented operational incidents near this site: {value}.
heritage.documented-hazard-or-rover-trav.explain: Real missions log surprises such as wheels slipping in soft soil, rovers trapped in shadow, or communication outages. These logs offer practical lessons that models alone can miss.
heritage.documented-hazard-or-rover-trav.readIt: Recorded incidents nearby are warnings worth designing around; none recorded may simply mean no one has operated there yet.

heritage.nearby-active-planned-missions-.lead: Other active or planned missions operating near this site: {value}.
heritage.nearby-active-planned-missions-.explain: Spacecraft working close together must coordinate landing times, respect each other's exclusion zones, avoid radio interference and stay clear of landing debris, a bit like neighbours sharing a driveway and a Wi-Fi channel.
heritage.nearby-active-planned-missions-.readIt: No neighbours means simpler planning; nearby missions add coordination work but may also offer chances to cooperate.

heritage.cultural-heritage-preservation-.lead: Heritage protection status for this site: {value}.
heritage.cultural-heritage-preservation-.explain: Historic hardware on the Moon is treated much like an archaeological site, and NASA's 2011 guidance asks new landers to touch down at least 2 km away so exhaust does not damage or contaminate it. This tool applies that guidance as a general courtesy buffer.
heritage.cultural-heritage-preservation-.readIt: A site well clear of any buffer needs no special care; one inside it would need a different landing point or extra permissions.
